candidates.title: Draft delayed-shipment alerts

demandEvidence.chore: Prepare a draft dispatcher alert from an operator-supplied shipment status marked delayed.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: A simple flow can notify a dispatcher when a shipment is delayed

ease.reason: A synthetic status and message template make a first mock approachable; no supplied reference documents alert tooling.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small logistics operators may pay for clearer delay notices; the discussion establishes no buying intent.

feasibility.reason: A four-week test can draft from sample statuses; live carrier access and delivery are unverified.

autonomy.reason: A repeatable draft is possible on supplied status, but a human must verify and send; automation is undocumented.

evidence.reason: The retained task span names a delayed-shipment alert but gives no fields, frequency, or corroboration.

experimentPlan.output: A concise draft alert for a shipment marked delayed, with the status and next check clearly shown.
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator marks a fictional shipment status as delayed.
steps: Read the supplied status and identifier.
Check that the status equals the operator-defined delayed value.
Fill a short alert template with the supplied facts.
Show the draft and source fields for review.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For labeled fictional delayed and on-time inputs, draft an alert only for delayed cases and copy the identifier and status correctly.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: An operator must define the delayed rule, supply status data, verify the draft, and send any real message.

candidates.reason: Below threshold: a proposed mock is narrow, but the source is a single example and no implementation support or buyer validation is supplied.

candidates.title: Compare a freemium app pricing idea

demandEvidence.chore: Review a freemium app concept and compare possible monetization models.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: I'm an indie app dev and looking for some conceptual help with one of my freemium apps

ease.reason: A student can make a structured comparison from supplied fictional app details, but the input framework is a proposal.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: indie app developers may pay for monetization advice; one request provides no validated buyer evidence.

feasibility.reason: A four-week manual prototype can compare a few options; useful evaluation criteria and outcomes remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: The proposed output is repeatable but depends on human supplied facts and judgment; no automation is documented.

evidence.reason: The post requests conceptual help for a freemium app but supplies no app details, recurrence, or corroboration.

experimentPlan.output: A short comparison of three possible freemium monetization models against operator-supplied app goals and constraints.
experimentPlan.trigger: An app developer submits a concept and asks for monetization options.
steps: Extract only the supplied goals and constraints.
List three plausible model options as hypotheses.
Compare tradeoffs against each supplied goal.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On a fictional app brief with known goals, produce three options and verify each comparison references a stated goal while labeling assumptions.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person supplies accurate app context, reviews the options, and makes business decisions; no model recommendation is validated.
unverified: Accuracy of operator supplied market assumptions
Any real buyer willingness to pay

candidates.reason: Below threshold: the request is concrete but broad and singular; no app context or evidence that this advice can predict outcomes.

candidates.title: Organize game-test CSV logs

demandEvidence.chore: Capture mobile game-test measurements in a log and transfer exported CSV rows into a Google Sheet without missed or duplicate files.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: I have tried a Schedule Trigger plus Google Drive Watch Files and also a Webhook from a shortcut on the phone, but the workflow either doesn’t fire at all or fires twice on the same file.

ease.reason: A table mock can be tested with fictional CSV rows, but file triggers are not documented in the supplied evidence.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small game-testing teams may pay for cleaner logs; this post shows one stated need, not payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week test can compare manually supplied rows and expected log entries; parsing and file intake remain unknown.

autonomy.reason: A person must export, upload, and check rows; no autonomous trigger or deduplication capability is established.

evidence.reason: Retained spans describe the current manual logging and repeated or missed file triggers, without corroborating demand.

experimentPlan.output: A review sheet that flags missing or repeated game-test CSV rows before a person pastes approved entries into a log.
inputs: Fictional CSV rows with battery, temperature, frame drops and notes
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator supplies an exported CSV and expected identifiers for review.
steps: Read the supplied rows and identifiers.
Check required fields against the chosen template.
Flag repeated identifiers under the operator rule.
Present a review table for manual correction and import.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For a labeled sample CSV, correctly flag seeded missing fields, repeated identifiers, and absent expected IDs without changing the source rows.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person exports and supplies the CSV, chooses matching rules, verifies flags, and performs any sheet update.
unverified: Actual CSV format and parser reliability
Reliable phone upload and file trigger behavior
Whether identifier deduplication fits the real log

candidates.reason: Below threshold: the chore and inputs are unusually clear, but the proposed review only addresses supplied files; the described trigger failure and live sheet automation remain outside supported scope.

candidates.title: Check Meta and Shopify purchase totals

demandEvidence.chore: Export comparable daily Meta purchase and Shopify order totals for 30 days and investigate unusual differences.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: In Shopify, export daily orders for the same 30 days, Online Store channel only, without test and cancelled orders.

ease.reason: A spreadsheet comparison using operator supplied totals is accessible; no supplied reference supports a live connector.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small online shops may pay for clearer ad-sales reconciliation; a single guide does not validate buyers.

feasibility.reason: A four-week test can compare fictional daily totals and flag large gaps; attribution interpretation remains human work.

autonomy.reason: A repeated comparison can flag dates, but a person must export, interpret causes, and check tracking settings.

evidence.reason: The retained spans give specific export instructions and possible discrepancy explanations, but no recurrence or corroboration.

experimentPlan.output: A table that aligns daily Meta and Shopify totals and flags dates with unusually large gaps for human investigation.
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator supplies aligned daily totals for a selected 30-day period.
steps: Check both tables cover the same dates.
Calculate the absolute and relative difference using a stated rule.
Flag dates above the operator threshold.
List possible checks as questions, not diagnoses.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For a synthetic aligned dataset with seeded gaps, verify date matching and flag exactly the dates that cross the chosen threshold.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person exports the reports, chooses a threshold, checks flagged dates and investigates pixels or attribution; the tool must not declare a cause.
unverified: Whether the proposed flags reduce useful review effort

candidates.reason: Below threshold: the task is specific enough for a synthetic comparison, but one how-to post does not establish repeat need, buyer intent, or a supported live integration.

rejected.reason: The retained excerpt says stories were invented and asks how outcomes might change, but does not identify a concrete operational chore or requested service; proposing one would invent demand.

rejected.title: Screen-time eye fatigue checker
rejected.reason: This is a maker explanation for an existing eye-blink fatigue tool and personal motivation, not a distinct unmet chore or request for a service. No health-administration proposal is supported.

rejected.title: Shopify app review advice
rejected.reason: The only retained text asks for advice about the review process; it supplies no specific task, blocker, or requested output from which to scope an experiment.

rejected.title: Weekly keyword-volume workflow
rejected.reason: The retained span documents a scheduled keyword-volume workflow and setup, not a user chore or unmet request. The schedule sentence alone is not demand for a distinct service.

rejected.title: Chatbot and booking services listing
rejected.reason: The retained span advertises an existing provider’s chatbot and booking services; it does not identify a separate requester’s unmet chore. Repackaging that listing as demand would overstate evidence.

rejected.title: Conversation blindspot detector
rejected.reason: The retained excerpt describes a maker’s existing conversation-analysis tool, not an unmet chore or request for a distinct service. It does not establish demand for a competing proposal.

steps.message: Assessed all ten sealed discussion assignments. Four concrete bounded chores received proposed plans and five provisional scores; each remains below the six-point mean threshold. Six assignments were excluded because retained evidence did not establish a distinct concrete chore. No post proposed.
